title: What is the difference between Databricks `OPTIMIZE` and `VACUUM` — OPTIMIZE compacts small files and optionally applies ZORDER; VACUUM removes old unreferenced files beyond the retention period (default 7 days) to reclaim storage — and why must you not VACUUM below the retention period (breaks time travel)?
shortTitle: What is the difference between Databricks `OPTIMIZE` and `VACUUM`

s1_definition.profdef: `OPTIMIZE` and `VACUUM` are two Delta Lake maintenance commands that address different problems. `OPTIMIZE` compacts many small data files into fewer larger ones to improve read performance, and can optionally co-locate related data with `ZORDER BY` to improve data skipping on filter columns. `VACUUM` permanently deletes old data files that are no longer referenced by the current table version and are older than a retention threshold, reclaiming storage, and because it physically removes files it also removes the ability to time travel to versions that relied on those files, which is why vacuuming below the default seven-day retention is dangerous.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India stores its trade records as a huge number of loose slips in filing drawers. `OPTIMIZE` is like a clerk who gathers thousands of tiny loose slips and neatly binds them into a few thick, well-organized folders, so finding records later is far faster, and the ZORDER part is like also sorting those folders by the fields you most often search on, like date and symbol, so you can skip whole folders. `VACUUM` is a completely different clerk, the shredder operator, who goes through the archive room and permanently shreds old discarded drafts that are no longer part of the current records and are older than a safety window. The warning is that if you shred too aggressively, below the safety window, you destroy the old drafts that the time-machine feature relied on to reconstruct how the records looked last week, so you can no longer go back in time.
s1_definition.oneliner: `OPTIMIZE` compacts small files and can ZORDER for faster reads, while `VACUUM` permanently deletes old unreferenced files to save storage, and vacuuming below the retention window breaks time travel because it destroys the historical files.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `OPTIMIZE` and `VACUUM` are two Delta Lake maintenance commands that address different problems. `OPTIMIZE` compacts many small data files into fewer larger ones to improve read performance, and can optionally co-locate related data with `ZORDER BY` to improve data skipping on filter columns. `VACUUM` permanently deletes old data files that are no longer referenced by the current table version and are older than a retention threshold, reclaiming storage, and because it physically removes files it also removes the ability to time travel to versions that relied on those files, which is why vacuuming below the default seven-day retention is dangerous.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India stores its trade records as a huge number of loose slips in filing drawers. `OPTIMIZE` is like a clerk who gathers thousands of tiny loose slips and neatly binds them into a few thick, well-organized folders, so finding records later is far faster, and the ZORDER part is like also sorting those folders by the fields you most often search on, like date and symbol, so you can skip whole folders. `VACUUM` is a completely different clerk, the shredder operator, who goes through the archive room and permanently shreds old discarded drafts that are no longer part of the current records and are older than a safety window. The warning is that if you shred too aggressively, below the safety window, you destroy the old drafts that the time-machine feature relied on to reconstruct how the records looked last week, so you can no longer go back in time.

**One line to remember:** `OPTIMIZE` compacts small files and can ZORDER for faster reads, while `VACUUM` permanently deletes old unreferenced files to save storage, and vacuuming below the retention window breaks time travel because it destroys the historical files.

sections.s2_technical:
Delta Lake tables accumulate many small files over time, especially from streaming writes, frequent small batches, or high-cardinality partitioning. Many small files hurt reads because the engine pays metadata and task-scheduling overhead per file and cannot scan efficiently, which is the classic small-files problem. `OPTIMIZE table` fixes this by reading the small files in each partition and rewriting them into a smaller number of larger files, typically around the ideal file size of a few hundred megabytes, without changing the data. This is a compaction operation: the row contents are identical, just packed into fewer files, so subsequent reads are faster. Optionally you add `ZORDER BY (col1, col2)`, which physically reorders the data within the files so that rows with similar values of those columns sit together, dramatically improving data skipping: Delta keeps per-file min and max statistics, and when your query filters on a Z-ordered column the engine can skip files whose min-max range cannot match, reading far less data. You Z-order on the columns you filter on most, such as trade date and symbol.

`VACUUM` solves a different problem: reclaiming storage. Because Delta is versioned, every update, delete, or optimize writes new files and leaves the old files on storage so that time travel and concurrent readers still work. Over time these superseded files pile up and cost money. `VACUUM table` permanently deletes data files that are no longer referenced by the current table version and are older than the retention period, which defaults to seven days. Crucially, it does not touch files that the current version still references, and it respects the retention window to protect readers and time travel. The retention threshold exists precisely because time travel to an older version requires the files that version pointed to; if you vacuum away files newer than the retention, you can delete files that a recent historical version still needs, so a time-travel query to that version fails, and in-flight long-running readers can break. That is why Delta refuses by default to vacuum with a retention shorter than seven days unless you explicitly override a safety check, and overriding it is a known foot-gun.

A senior-level nuance is the interaction between the two: optimize creates new compacted files and leaves the old small files as unreferenced history, so storage temporarily grows after optimize, and vacuum is what eventually reclaims that space once the old files age past retention. So the healthy maintenance pattern is to optimize regularly for read performance and to vacuum periodically for storage, with the retention set to cover your required time-travel window. Another nuance is that optimize is safe to run anytime and only improves reads, while vacuum is destructive and irreversible for the files it removes, so you size the retention to your business and compliance needs, for example keeping thirty days if auditors may need to reconstruct a month of history, and you never shorten it just to save a little storage. On Databricks there are also automatic options, like auto-compaction and optimized writes that reduce small files at write time, and predictive optimization that manages this for you, but understanding the manual commands and the retention rule is essential. The practical banking rule is optimize for speed, vacuum for space, and treat the retention period as a safety boundary that protects time travel and must match your audit requirements.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the trades Delta table is written by a streaming job that produces thousands of tiny files per day. After a few weeks, analytical queries over the table became slow because the engine had to open an enormous number of small files. This is exactly the problem optimize solves: compacting the many small files into a few large ones restores read performance, and Z-ordering by trade date and symbol lets queries skip files that cannot match their filters.

This is exactly how optimize works. It rewrites the small files into fewer larger ones without changing the data, and ZORDER co-locates rows so min-max data skipping becomes effective.

Problem 2 — All those superseded small files, plus the pre-compaction files left behind by optimize, accumulated on storage and the bill grew. Vacuum reclaims that space by deleting old unreferenced files, but the audit team requires the ability to time travel back thirty days to reconstruct the table for any day in the past month. So the retention must be at least thirty days, and vacuuming below that would delete files the time-travel feature needs and break it.

Because we cannot run real Delta maintenance, this runnable demo models the file lifecycle. A `DeltaStorage` tracks data files, which version references them, and their age. An `Optimizer` compacts a partition's small files into one large file, leaving the old files unreferenced, and simulates Z-order skipping. A `Vacuumer` deletes unreferenced files older than the retention and refuses to vacuum below the safety window, showing how an unsafe vacuum would break a time-travel read. The demo writes many small files, optimizes them, reads with Z-order skipping, then vacuums safely and shows an unsafe vacuum breaking time travel.

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml
delta:
  optimize:
    target-file-size-mb: 256
    zorder-by: [trade_date, symbol]
  vacuum:
    retention-hours: 720          # 30 days (audit requires 30-day time travel)
    default-retention-hours: 168  # 7 days default safety
    enforce-retention-check: true
```

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -cp target/delta-maintenance-sim-1.0.0.jar com.bank.maint.MaintenanceDemo

# Real Databricks SQL:
#   OPTIMIZE banking_prod.trades.settlements ZORDER BY (trade_date, symbol);
#   VACUUM banking_prod.trades.settlements RETAIN 720 HOURS;   -- 30 days
#   -- NEVER: VACUUM ... RETAIN 1 HOURS  (needs spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled=false; breaks time travel)
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a Delta trades table with six tiny files written by streaming at version zero, each covering a small key range and all about thirty-three days old, with an audit requirement to time travel back thirty days.

Step 1: Before optimize, the table has six small referenced files, which is the small-files problem that slows reads.

Step 2: Optimize reads the six small files and compacts them into one large file at a new version. The six old small files are marked unreferenced, kept as history for now, and the new compacted file becomes the only referenced file. Because the data was Z-ordered by trade date and symbol, the compacted file carries min and max statistics that enable data skipping.

Step 3: After optimize the table has one referenced file but seven total files on storage, because the six old small files still sit there as history, which is why storage temporarily grows after an optimize.

Step 4: A filtered read for a specific key uses the min and max statistics to decide which files to scan. With the compacted Z-ordered file covering the needed range, only the matching file is scanned and the rest would be skipped.

Step 5: A vacuum is attempted with a retention of one hour. Because one hour is below the seven-day safety window and the safety override is off, the vacuum is refused, with a log explaining that vacuuming below retention would delete files recent versions reference and break time travel.

Step 6: A vacuum is then run with the thirty-day retention. The six old small files are older than thirty days, so they are deleted and storage is reclaimed. As a consequence, a time-travel read to version zero now fails because its files were removed, while a read of the current version still works since its compacted file remains. This illustrates the exact trade-off: vacuum reclaims space but destroys the ability to time travel to versions whose files it deleted, so the retention must match the audit window.

Final output:

```

INFO: Before OPTIMIZE: 6 small referenced files
INFO: OPTIMIZE compacting 6 small files into 1 large file
INFO: ZORDER BY (trade_date, symbol) applied — per-file min/max now enable data skipping
INFO: After OPTIMIZE: 1 referenced file(s), 7 total files on storage
INFO: Query filter key=25 scanned 1 file(s) (skipped the rest)
SEVERE: VACUUM REFUSED: retention 1h < safety 168h. Vacuuming below retention would DELETE files that recent versions reference → breaks time travel.
INFO: VACUUM removed 6 old unreferenced files (reclaimed storage)
INFO: Time travel to version 0 → FAILED (files vacuumed)
INFO: Time travel to version 1 → OK (files present)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Optimize and vacuum are two Delta Lake maintenance commands that solve different problems, and I keep them clearly separate. Optimize is about read speed: it compacts many small data files into fewer larger ones, which fixes the small-files problem that comes from streaming writes and frequent small batches, because the engine otherwise pays metadata and scheduling overhead per file. Optionally you add ZORDER BY on the columns you filter on most, like trade date and symbol, which physically co-locates rows with similar values so that Delta's per-file min and max statistics let queries skip files that cannot match, reading far less data. Optimize does not change the data, it just packs it better, so it is non-destructive and safe to run anytime.

Vacuum is about reclaiming storage. Because Delta is versioned, every update, delete, or optimize writes new files and leaves the superseded files on storage so time travel and concurrent readers still work, and over time those old files pile up and cost money. Vacuum permanently deletes data files that the current version no longer references and that are older than the retention period, which defaults to seven days. It never touches files the current version still needs. The critical rule is that vacuuming below the retention window is dangerous, because time travel to an older version requires the files that version pointed to, so if you delete files newer than the retention you can remove files a recent historical version still references, which makes time-travel queries to that version fail and can break in-flight readers. That is why Delta refuses by default to vacuum with a retention shorter than seven days unless you override a safety check, and overriding it is a well-known foot-gun.

At the National Bank of India our streaming job wrote thousands of tiny files to the trades table each day, and after a few weeks analytical queries slowed down badly, so we scheduled optimize with ZORDER by trade date and symbol, which compacted the files and made filtered queries skip most of them. Those superseded files, plus the pre-compaction files optimize left behind, grew our storage bill, so we also scheduled vacuum, but the audit team required the ability to time travel back thirty days, so we set the retention to thirty days and never shortened it. The mental model I carry is optimize for speed, vacuum for space, storage temporarily grows right after an optimize because the old files linger until they age past retention, and the retention period is a safety boundary that protects time travel and must match the compliance window, so you never shorten it just to save a little storage.
